rounds.plain: The proposed differentiated rules corpus and reviewed edge cases are not evidenced. A maintained rules engine could qualify in principle, but free official tools and close competitors leave the advantage unproven.

The check found neither two dated launches since 23 Apr 2026 nor five low-priced maintained incumbents covering the combined ITAR workflow. This result predates or is contradicted by the later deep-evidence finding of ExChek’s 28 April 2026 launch.

risks: No verified revenue, paid-customer counts, search demand or user adoption were found; listed prices are not proof of payment.
Acceptance of automated classification without expert review is unverified; ITAR Screen calls results preliminary and recommends qualified counsel.
A UK-based founder's access to controlled technical data may complicate cloud operation; the source says to validate the architecture with qualified counsel.
The proposed rules corpus and edge-case review are not an established durable advantage.
records.moat: A maintained, versioned rules engine could qualify in principle, but the rules are largely based on public regulations and official lists, and close competitors and free BIS tools exist. The source describes the moat as weak and not yet demonstrated; customer-history switching costs are possible but weakened by exportable records.

hours.value: Unverified; no operating evidence that the product can stay within 5 hours per week.
hours.note: Human review for ambiguous classifications, regulatory changes and customer escalations may exceed the limit.

records.next_steps: Run a one-workday desk test without cold outreach: check exact-intent search volume and CPC, compare several synthetic publicly documented product descriptions across BIS, ITAR Screen and ExChek, and record mismatches, citations and human-review needs. If material gaps appear, create a no-code page with a clear price and opt-in waitlist.

rounds.plain: The maintained dataset and rules engine have not been built. A source-linked directory could become a data asset if maintained, but public information is reproducible and existing providers and free government alternatives limit the current advantage.

The check found no post-cutoff launch or five reviewed low-price exact lookup incumbents, and treated a maintained state-and-locality directory as a possible data asset. Later deep evidence describes adjacent alternatives, including LegalZoom, Foundra and free government tools.

risks: No verified product revenue, paid conversion, churn or support burden was found.
Exact target-market size and search demand are unverified.
Free state and SST registration tools exist, and some sellers may not need separate registration in particular situations.
A broad licensing scope creates substantial accuracy and maintenance work; the source says independent build-hour and maintenance-hour estimates are unverified.
A report/export product may have weak repeat use without reliable change alerts.
records.moat: Conditional potential, not a current moat. A maintained, cited dataset with change history could qualify, but public state information is reproducible, incumbents and free government alternatives exist, and one-off lookup has little switching cost.

hours.value: Unverified; no operating product exists to measure.
hours.note: The ≤5h/week ceiling is not demonstrated, especially if human review is needed to keep requirements current.

records.next_steps: Run a one-day smoke test: create three source-linked state registration checklists and offer a manually delivered $19 PDF through a landing page and exact-intent Google Search ads with a small fixed spend cap. Count a non-friend completed purchase as the signal; clicks and waitlist signups alone do not validate willingness to pay.
